extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students/scholars of poetics and classical literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating classical poetic drama (especially tragedy): how to construct plot, choose meters and musical elements, shape characters and speeches, and achieve the tragic effect (pity/fear/catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and the imitative arts are fundamentally acts of imitation: men are by nature imitative and take pleasure in representations. Imitation may proceed by number (rhythm), harmony (music), and speech (oration/ metre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose by imitating actions and states of character through the appropriate instruments (rhythm, harmony, speech). Recognize that different arts use different instruments (e.g., painting uses colors, lyric uses voice), but all that properly are imitative aim to represent life and produce pleasure and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold difference in imitation (medium, objects, manner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative arts differ (1) in the medium or instruments they employ (number, harmony, speech), (2) in the objects they imitate (types of persons or actions), and (3) in the manner of imitation (whether by narrative or by enactment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing genre/technique, decide which instruments to use, which objects to represent, and whether the work will enact the action (drama) or tell it (epic). These choices determine which features (chorus, metre, spectacle) are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; it is effected by language embellished (with rhythm, harmony and metre), and by means of pity and fear effects the catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for seriousness and completeness in the action; use elevated yet fitting language (consider rhythm and musical elements); and shape events to arouse pity and fear, bringing about catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of tragedy are six: fabula (plot/composition of the action), mores (character), sententia (thought), elocutio (diction), melopoeia (melody/song), and apparatus (spectacle/stagecraft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each part distinctly: plot and character concern the persons and deeds imitated; thought and diction concern what is said and how; melody and apparatus are the musical and visual instruments. Plot is the foremost of these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (Fabula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot (fabula), the composition of the action, is the most important element in tragedy: tragedy is the imitation of action, not of men; the end (action) is the chief good of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize coherent arrangement of incidents into a single, unified action. Even excellent diction or character-sketches cannot replace a well-constructed plot. When composing, begin with the plot (the soul of the drama) before polishing speeches or stagecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and completeness of action (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete action has a beginning, middle and end: a beginning is that which does not necessarily follow anything else, an end is that after which nothing follows, and a middle is that which follows and is followed of necessity or usually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots so that incidents follow by necessity or probability; avoid beginnings or endings that are random. The action should be whole (one coherent sequence), not a mere collection of episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single action requirement (avoid episodic/episodic plots)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should represent one single, complete action, not many separate actions or an episodic series of loosely connected incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject 'episodic' or 'epilogic' plots where episodes are merely stitched together without causal or probable connection. Each incident should contribute to the unity of the one action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and appropriate length
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must have a magnitude (size/length) suitable for the effect: not so small as to be insignificant, nor so large as to be ungraspable; large enough for its entirety to be apprehended and remembered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a scope that allows a single coherent action to be intelligible in performance and memory. Magnitude is tied to the capacity to produce the tragic effect when the whole is perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex versus simple plots; role of peripeteia and agnitio
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots (those including peripeteia — a reversal — and agnitio — recognition) are superior; peripeteia is a sudden reversal of fortune, agnitio is the shift from ignorance to knowledge, ideally simultaneous with reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate reversals and recognitions that arise naturally from the plot (causally/probably) to maximize pity and fear. The most moving episodes are those where recognition and reversal occur together (example: Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal necessity or probability (no reliance on chance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia, agnitio, and all decisive incidents should arise from the constitution of the plot itself — from prior events by necessity or probability — not by mere chance or externally grafted episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that key turns and revelations are motivated by earlier facts of the plot; accidental or post hoc devices weaken the unity and verisimilitude and lessen tragic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic effect: pity, fear, and catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of tragedy is to arouse pity and fear by representing dreadful and pitiful actions, and through such emotions to effect a catharsis (purging or purgation) of these passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape incidents, character vulnerability, and reversals to move the audience to pity and fear. Prefer plots where misfortune arises not from vice or depravity alone but through complex causes that elicit compassion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Mores) subordinate but necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is a constituent part of tragedy: characters should be consistent and appropriate, but character alone is inferior to plot; the incidents an agent performs (action) define the tragic work more than their moral traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters believable and their actions consistent with character, yet always subordinate to the needs of the plot. Good character supports the plausibility of actions that produce pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Sententia) and Diction (Elocutio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is appropriate to the situation (statements, arguments) and is akin to political and rhetorical skill; diction is the expression — the proper and fitting wording and meter for speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft speeches that fit the characters and the situation; use appropriate rhetorical devices and meters (iambic often suits familiar speech in drama). Diction must serve the action and reveal thought without overshadowing the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melopoeia (music/chorus) and Apparatus (spectacle) as adjuncts
rubrics_metrics.description: Melopoeia (musical element, choral song and rhythm) and apparatus (stagecraft, spectacle) are parts of tragedy: melody is a chief embellishment while spectacle, though powerful in effect, is the least proper to poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use musical and choral components to enhance emotional effect but not as substitutes for plot. Treat spectacle as external aid — potentially moving but not the primary source of poetic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre distinctions and appropriate metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poetic genres have different instruments: epic (epopoeia) imitates by narrative in hexameter and without musical harmony; tragedy and comedy imitate by acting with metres and, in tragedy, with rhythm, harmony and metre; comedy tends to imitate the inferior, the ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the genre-appropriate metre and musical form: epic often uses hexameter and allows long, indefinite scope; tragedy should adopt metres suited to spoken/acted language (e.g., iambic for familiar speech) and mix metres where needed. Do not confuse the modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictionalization and universality over strict historicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry differs from history: the historian reports what happened (singular facts), the poet shows what sort of things could or must happen (the universal). Poets may invent names and particulars so long as events are probable or necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not feel bound to historical names or strict factual accuracy; prioritize the universal truth of the action (what kinds of things happen) and verisimilitude. Fictitious particulars are acceptable if they serve the unity and believability of the plot.
